posts.caption: In 2021, one engineer typed one wrong command and 3.5 billion people lost the internet in a single instant. Not hacked. Not attacked. Just one wrong line of code during a routine maintenance check. Facebook's own engineers couldn't even log in to fix it, their access tools were on the same servers that just vanished. They had to physically drive to data centers and override servers by hand. One by one. 6 hours. $60 million lost every single hour. And the exact same vulnerability? Still exists right now. The internet is more fragile than you think.

2021 mein ek engineer ne ek galat command type ki aur 3.5 billion logon ka internet ek pal mein band ho gaya. Hack nahi hua. Attack nahi hua. Bas ek routine maintenance check ke dauran ek galat line of code. 6 ghante. Har ghante 60 million dollar ka nuksaan. Internet utna strong nahi jitna hum sochte hain.

There is a sound that only 2% of people can hear. Scientists have studied it for 50 years and still have no answer. It's called The Hum — and the leading theory is that it's the Earth itself vibrating at a frequency most humans aren't built to detect. A woman heard it for 11 years, moved across the country to escape it, and it followed her to the new house. Stop right now, close your eyes, and listen. What do you hear?

We call space the final frontier. But we've barely explored our own planet. Earth is stranger than anything we've found out there — and most people have no idea. From perfect solar eclipses to oceans deeper than mountains are tall, this is the planet you thought you knew.

In 1974, a man calculated the exact day he would die and spent a year preparing for it. What happened next is stranger than the prediction itself. Frank was obsessed with numerology. He told his family, quit his job, and gave away everything he owned. When the day came and went without incident, he thought he'd beaten fate. He hadn't.

This toxic chemotherapy agent is a hero and a villain of this story, but it absolutely saved his life.

Where did the antimatter go? The Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated each other instantly. So why does anything exist at all? Scientists are still hunting for the missing half of reality.

What we know about human history is only a fraction of the full story. Much of the rest is like dark matter, invisible to us. We can’t see it, and we can only see the effects of its presence. recentPosts.caption:
Photographer captured these incredible aerial videos at Lake Maharloo near Shiraz, Iran, where thousands of flamingos gather among waters that can turn shades of pink, red, and orange.⁠
⁠
From above, the birds become tiny dots, lines, and shapes moving across the pink, red, orange, and green water. ⁠
⁠
The colors change with the seasons as evaporation increases the lake’s salt concentration and creates conditions for microorganisms and algae that give the water its striking colors. ⁠
⁠
By: @hose

A mini train, your own controls and a whole lot of fun! 🚂🇯🇵⁠
At The Railway Museum in Saitama, Japan, you can actually drive your own miniature train, explore interactive exhibits and try out some pretty cool railway simulations.⁠
⁠
If you're planning a visit, make sure to book the mini train experience in advance, spots are limited!⁠
Definitely a museum worth adding to your Japan itinerary. ⁠
🎥: @via.kat

@dario.nyc and @frjframes captured Auvers-sur-Oise, the small French village where Vincent van Gogh spent the final weeks of his life.⁠
⁠
He arrived in May 1890 and stayed for just over two months. In that short time, he painted over 70 works, including The Church at Auvers and Wheatfield with Crows. ⁠
⁠
Many of the places he painted still look remarkably similar today.

A little beauty secret straight from nature. 🌹💄⁠
In Peru, one of the most iconic red pigments has a rather unexpected origin: tiny insects called cochineal that live on prickly pear cacti.⁠
⁠
When dried and processed, these insects produce carminic acid, which creates carmine, a rich natural red dye used for centuries in cosmetics, textiles and food coloring.⁠
⁠
So the next time you reach for a bold red lipstick, remember that its color might have a very surprising story behind it. ⁠
🎥: @liya

This sand cat was photographed with her kittens in Kuwait, a rare sight, since these shy desert cats are incredibly hard to spot 🐾⁠
⁠
Their sandy fur blends perfectly into the desert, and they’re mostly active at night, which makes them even harder to find. For the photographer, these images were the most special moments he captured all year 🤍⁠
⁠
Have you ever seen a sand cat before? ⁠
⁠
By: @talal92

Who knew taking the subway could feel like visiting an art gallery? 😍🚇⁠
Stockholm’s metro is famous for its incredible underground art, with stations transformed into colorful spaces featuring murals, sculptures, installations and unique designs. ⁠
⁠
Often called the world’s longest art gallery, the network showcases works by more than 150 artists across dozens of stations.⁠
🎥: @burcuyaran

@hugoraphy, a nature photographer from Finland, captured these breathtaking winter scenes that show just how magical the season can be ❄️⁠
⁠
From starry skies above untouched snow to quiet frozen landscapes, each photo feels like stepping into a winter dream.⁠
⁠
Which of these winter moments would you love to experience in person?

What if a musical instrument could sound like an animal? 🐦🎶⁠
These fascinating instruments are called ocarinas. Made in different shapes, some are designed to imitate animal calls, turning music into something that sounds almost like nature itself.⁠
⁠
You can discover these unusual instruments at the Machu Picchu Museum in Cusco, Peru, where they offer a glimpse into the region’s rich pre-Columbian musical traditions.⁠
⁠
A little piece of history you can actually hear!⁠
🎥: @brendajuliam

At The Fat Duck in England, one of the most famous dishes comes with its own soundtrack.⁠
⁠
It’s called “Sound of the Sea.” The plate looks like a tiny beach, with edible “sand,” seafood, and seaweed, and before you eat, you put on headphones playing crashing waves and seagulls.⁠
⁠
Created by chef Heston Blumenthal, it’s part of a three-Michelin-star tasting menu where every course is designed to feel like a journey.⁠
⁠
By: @thefatduck

Nature really said no lip filler needed! 👀🐒💗⁠
⁠
Meet the Yunnan snub-nosed monkey, one of China's most distinctive and endangered primates. ⁠
Recognisable by its striking pink lips, tiny upturned nose and thick golden-black fur, this rare species lives in the high-altitude forests of Yunnan Province, including the mountainous areas around Shangri-La.⁠
⁠
They spend much of their lives in the treetops, travelling through mountain forests in large social groups. With their unusual features and l

A beautiful sight with a meaning that goes far beyond its colors. 🏔️⁠
These Tibetan prayer flags are printed with sacred mantras, prayers and symbols. Traditionally hung across mountain passes, temples and rooftops, they are believed to spread positive energy and blessings as the wind moves through them.⁠
⁠
Each flag represents a wish for happiness, compassion, good fortune and peace for all living beings. ⁠
A tradition that turns even the simplest breeze into a message of hope.⁠
🎥: @dazerener
